title: Future Continuous & Future Perfect
subtitle: Two ways to describe the future from a specific point in time: in progress, or already finished.
objectives: Review the future continuous (in progress at a future moment)
Form and use the future perfect (will have + past participle)
Tell the two apart based on whether the action is finished or ongoing at that future point

content.intro: Picture a specific moment in the future — say, next Friday at noon. Will something still be happening then, or will it already be finished? That's the choice between these two tenses.

rules.heading: a) Future continuous (review)
rules.body:
will be + -ing = still happening at that future moment.

  • At noon, I will be traveling. (in progress at that moment)

rules.heading: b) Future perfect
rules.body:
will have + past participle = already finished by that future moment.

  • By noon, I will have arrived. (finished before or exactly at that moment)
  • By next year, she will have graduated.

rules.heading: c) Telling them apart
rules.body: Future continuous answers "what will be happening?"; future perfect answers "what will already be done?" — the key signal word is often "by" (future perfect) vs. a moment in time alone (future continuous).

examples: At noon, I will be traveling.
By noon, I will have arrived.
This time next week, we will be relaxing on the beach.
By next year, she will have graduated.
By the time you read this, I will have left.
At 8pm, they will still be working.

commonMistakes.wrong: By tomorrow, I will finishing the report.
commonMistakes.right: By tomorrow, I will have finished the report.
commonMistakes.why: "By" + a future point signals completion — use the future perfect (will have + past participle).

commonMistakes.wrong: At noon, I will have traveling.
commonMistakes.right: At noon, I will be traveling.
commonMistakes.why: An action still in progress at that moment needs the future continuous (will be + -ing).

commonMistakes.wrong: By next year, she will have graduate.
commonMistakes.right: By next year, she will have graduated.
commonMistakes.why: The future perfect needs the past participle (graduated), not the base form.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Choose the future continuous or future perfect.

items.explanation: "By" signals completion before that point — future perfect.
In progress at that exact moment — future continuous.

items.prompt: This time next week, we ___ (relax) on the beach.
items.explanation: In progress at that specific moment — future continuous.

items.prompt: By the time you read this, I ___.
items.explanation: "By the time" signals completion — future perfect.
"Still" signals an ongoing action at that moment — future continuous.

items.incorrect: By tomorrow, I will finish the report. (emphasizing it will be done by then)
answer: By tomorrow, I will have finished the report.
items.explanation: "By" needs the future perfect to express "already done."

items.incorrect: By next year, she will have graduate.
answer: By next year, she will have graduated.
items.explanation: The future perfect needs the past participle.

summary: Future continuous (will be + -ing) = still happening at that future moment.
Future perfect (will have + past participle) = already finished by that future moment.
"By" / "by the time" are strong signals for the future perfect.
